question: How can repeating fragments, each with its own register and rhythm, add up to a landscape?
intro: The set ends with bells of many sizes, each a short figure that repeats, written on three staves. One broad melody sings in the middle, and one low chord tolls at the end. Same Lviv performance as the rest of Miroirs.

sections.label: B′ · Très calme returns
sections.mNote: calm chords return after the melody, in four sharps

sections.label: A′ · The carillon returns
sections.mNote: opening carillon returns; low rolled chords toll, fading to silence

cues.title: Two bells, then a carillon
cues.text: Très lent, quarter note = 50, pianissimo, on three staves. Two high G♯ octaves ring first, staggered between the hands. About 0:10 a stream of sextuplets starts in the right hand, marked très doux et sans accentuation: a carillon, over which the other bells will enter.
cues.evidence: The level rises from −32.2 dB at 0:05 to −18.7 dB at 0:10 and the attack rate from 0.6 to 4.2 a second; the report’s boundary at 0:12 scores 1.00, the strongest in the recording. The tempo, the three staves, the two staggered octaves and the sextuplets from bar 3 are on scan p. 44 of the first edition (IMSLP #02693) and in Kyle Fyr, Music Theory Online 26.4 (2020), paragraph 12.

cues.title: An accented bell
cues.text: In the loudest 5-second window of the recording, near 0:25, an accented mezzo-forte bell in the middle register, three repeated E♯s, cuts through the pianissimo. Kyle Fyr places it at the exact midpoint of these first eleven bars, forty-four beats long.
cues.evidence: The report lists 0:25 as the loudest 5-second window (−7.3 dB). The mf accent in the middle staff is on scan p. 44 (system 3). Fyr (paragraphs 13 and 23) identifies the accented bell and puts it halfway through the 44-beat first section; at beat 22 and about 0:25 the performance is close to the marked tempo of 50.

cues.title: A letter from Alkmaar
cues.text: Ravel dedicated this piece to Maurice Delage, his pupil and friend. In June 1905, on holiday in the Netherlands, he wrote to Delage about a cheese market at Alkmaar with carillons ringing ceaselessly, and windmills to the horizon: a mechanical landscape in which you could believe yourself an automaton.
cues.evidence: The letter is quoted in Kyle Fyr, Music Theory Online 26.4 (2020), paragraph 3, citing Orenstein, A Ravel Reader (2003), pp. 69–70. The dedication is on IMSLP’s work page; Delage’s friendship with Ravel and membership of the Apaches are in Wikipedia’s Les Apaches article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Apaches), and Jane Vial Jaffe’s programme note describes him as Ravel’s pupil.

cues.title: After the fermata, très calme
cues.text: A held chord ends the first section. At about 0:54 slow chords marked très calme and pp take over, in 6/4 and 3/4 over a low bass. Fyr hears the tolling parallel fourths carry across the join, so one bell links the two sections.
cues.evidence: The report’s boundary at 0:54 scores 0.88; the level and attack rate dip at 0:50 (−21.1 dB, 0.4 a second) before the new chords at 0:55 (−13.3 dB). The fermata bar, the très calme marking and the 6/4 and 3/4 bars are on scan p. 45. The carried-over fourths are Fyr’s reading (paragraph 16).

cues.title: Flats, and an accent halfway
cues.text: At about 1:12 the four sharps end. A double bar brings flats and a 5/4 bar with accented mezzo-forte notes. In Fyr’s count an accented bell sounds exactly halfway through this section, as it did in the first.
cues.evidence: The report has boundaries at 1:08 (0.77), 1:12 (0.68) and 1:16 (0.74), and its key estimate moves from C♯ (1:00–1:05) to G minor (1:10–1:15), a chroma-based guess. The double bar, the flats and the mf accented 5/4 bar are on scan p. 45 (system 3). Fyr (paragraph 23) puts the accent 17.5 beats into the 35-beat section.

cues.title: Largement chanté
cues.text: At about 1:36 Ravel writes largement chanté, broadly sung, mf, in flats. Fyr counts twelve bell sounds in the piece; eleven are short repeating figures, and this expansive melodic carillon is the exception.
cues.evidence: The level rises from −22.4 dB at 1:25 to −12.3 dB at 1:35, and the report has a boundary at 1:38 (0.81). The largement chanté marking and the new key signature are at the foot of scan p. 45. The count of twelve bell sounds, and the melodic exception, are in Fyr’s paragraph 15; Jane Vial Jaffe’s note also says a lush melody emerges only in the middle section.

cues.title: Bells at noon in Paris
cues.text: Ravel told the pianist Robert Casadesus that the piece was inspired by the bells that ring at noon in Paris. Roger Nichols calls it the only one of the five Miroirs that reflects a particular reality: the sound of midday bells.
cues.evidence: Fyr (paragraph 7) reports the remark to Casadesus, citing Marnat (1986), p. 184; Roger Nichols’s note for Hyperion CDA67731/2 (https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W5434_67731) makes the “only … particular reality” point.

cues.title: Rocking chords, then a swell
cues.text: From about 2:00 repeated rocking chords fill the middle staff under the melody, marked p calme, and the attack rate doubles. The line then swells: 2:35 and 2:45 are two of the five loudest windows of the whole recording.
cues.evidence: The report’s attack rate is 0.4–1.0 a second at 1:40–1:55 and 2.0–2.6 at 2:00–2:20, with a boundary at 2:00 (0.39). Its five loudest windows are 0:25, 3:55, 2:45, 0:35 and 2:35. The p calme rocking chords are on scan p. 46 (system 2) and the mf bars on scan pp. 46–47; exact bars are not aligned.

cues.title: A roll said to be Ravel
cues.text: A Duo-Art piano roll of this piece, made in 1922, was sold as played by Ravel. The player has not been conclusively identified: Ronald Woodley writes that the balance of probability favours the composer. Ravel admitted that a better pianist played some pieces in that roll collection.
cues.evidence: Fyr (paragraph 30) reports the roll, its 1922 sessions (citing Howat 2009, p. 321), Ravel’s letter to Calvocoressi about recruiting a better pianist (citing Orenstein 2003, p. 219) and Woodley’s judgement (2000, p. 222).

cues.title: A fermata, and the calm returns
cues.text: After the swell the level falls: −12.5 dB at 2:50, −20.9 at 3:25. A fermata chord stops the music, and at about 3:34 four sharps return with the très calme chords of the first calm section.
cues.evidence: The report has boundaries at 2:54 (0.97), 3:10 (0.96) and 3:34 (0.62); its attack rate falls to 0.2 a second at 3:25, and its key estimate at 3:35 is C♯ major (0.88), a chroma-based guess consistent with four sharps. The fermata chord, the new key signature and the très calme marking are at the foot of scan p. 47.

cues.title: An accent, then fading
cues.text: Around 3:55, the second loudest window of the whole recording, an accented mezzo-forte chord sounds in the calm section, and the sound then withdraws. Compare this accent with the one at about 1:12.
cues.evidence: The report lists 3:55 as the second loudest 5-second window (−7.7 dB), then −11.6 dB at 4:00 and −18.8 dB at 4:05. The mf accented chord and the following p and pp bars are on scan p. 48 (system 1).

cues.title: The carillon returns, with a low chord
cues.text: At about 4:10 the opening sextuplets return, pp, and within a few bars a low rolled chord, marked mf, sounds in the lowest staff. The recording’s level rises from −19 dB to −12 dB. This chord was not in the opening section; it first sounded in the middle of the piece.
cues.evidence: The report has a boundary at 4:02 (0.48), an attack rate of 2.6 a second at 4:10, and a level rise from −19.2 dB at 4:10 to −12.1 dB at 4:15. The pp sextuplets and the mf m.d. rolled chord are on scan p. 48 (systems 2–3); the chord’s exact bar is not aligned. Fyr (paragraph 22) identifies the rolled chord as a bell sound that first appears in the middle of the piece.

cues.title: La Savoyarde, and Faure’s lesson
cues.text: Ravel told the pianist Henriette Faure that the last chords stood for La Savoyarde, the great bell of Sacré-Cœur, installed in 1895. She recalled that he wanted the carillon and the high octave bells on two distinct levels, within a pianissimo that did not sound feeble.
cues.evidence: Fyr (paragraphs 10 and 29) reports both remarks, citing Henriette Faure, Mon maître Maurice Ravel (1978), pp. 77 and 79–80; Jane Vial Jaffe’s note repeats Faure’s coaching account.

cues.title: Four tolls, then silence
cues.text: The low rolled chord tolls four times, marked mf, mp, p, pp, and the last bar is silence under a fermata. In this recording the level falls from −12 dB at 4:15 to −26 dB at 4:35 and −41 dB at 4:40, the quietest window of the file.
cues.evidence: The report’s levels are −12.1 dB at 4:15, −25.7 dB at 4:35 and −41.2 dB at 4:40; 4:40 is the single quietest 5-second window in the report, and the file ends at 4:43. The four rolled chords marked mf, mp, p and pp and the final fermata bar are on scan p. 48 (systems 3–4).

transitions.title: A held chord, then slow chords
transitions.how: The carillon of sextuplets stops, and a chord under a fermata holds the last of the sound. Ravel then marks très calme and pp: slow chords in the middle staves over a low bass, in 4/4 and then 6/4 and 3/4. The four-sharp key signature does not change. In Kyle Fyr’s analysis the tolling fourths continue across the join while two new bells enter, so one bell connects the sections.
transitions.evidence: The report’s boundary at 0:54 scores 0.88; the level falls to −21.1 dB with an attack rate of 0.4 a second at 0:50, then rises to −13.3 dB at 0:55. The fermata bar, the très calme marking and the 6/4 and 3/4 bars are on scan p. 45 of the first edition (IMSLP #02693). The carried-over fourths are from Fyr, Music Theory Online 26.4 (2020), paragraph 16. The exact bar is not aligned.

transitions.title: The accents die away, then a melody
transitions.how: After the accented bars in flats, the writing thins to quiet chords above held bass notes, in 5/4, 4/4 and 6/4 bars. A double bar then brings a new set of flats and the marking largement chanté, mf: a melody in the right hand, broadly sung, over sustained chords in the other staves. The repeating bells recede, and a line that moves from note to note takes the foreground.
transitions.evidence: The level rises from −22.4 dB at 1:25 to −12.3 dB at 1:35, and the report has a boundary at 1:38 (0.81); its key estimate is F minor (0.79–0.84) at 1:40–1:45, a chroma-based guess. The thinning bars, the double bar, the new key signature and largement chanté are on scan p. 45 (systems 4–5). The exact bar is not aligned.

transitions.title: A fermata, and four sharps return
transitions.how: The melody falls away through quiet bars with long bass notes, p and then pp, and the level in the recording sinks towards silence. A chord under a fermata stops the sound. Ravel then changes the key signature from flats back to four sharps and marks très calme: the slow chords of the first calm section return, without the sung line.
transitions.evidence: The level falls from −12.5 dB at 2:50 to −20.9 dB at 3:25, the attack rate is 0.2 a second at 3:25, and the report has boundaries at 2:54 (0.97), 3:10 (0.96) and 3:34 (0.62). The quiet bars, the fermata chord, the four-sharp signature and très calme are on scan p. 47 (systems 4–5). The exact bar is not aligned.

transitions.title: Chords thin, and the carillon returns
transitions.how: The calm chords fall from mf to p and pp, and a bar of rests leaves the middle staves almost empty. Then the right hand restarts the sextuplets, pp, with the high G♯ octaves above, as in the first bars. Two bars of sextuplets later, a low rolled chord, mf, sounds in the lowest staff: the bell that first appeared in the middle of the piece. The opening returns with a heavier bell beneath it.
transitions.evidence: The level falls from −11.6 dB at 4:00 to −18.8 dB at 4:05; the report has a boundary at 4:02 (0.48), an attack rate of 2.6 a second at 4:10 and a level rise to −12.1 dB at 4:15. The p and pp chords, the rest bar, the returning sextuplets and the rolled chord are on scan p. 48 (systems 1–3). Fyr (paragraph 22) identifies the rolled chord. The exact bars are not aligned.

composer.epithet: An engineer of instrumental colour who made a piano imitate water, an orchestra imitate a machine, and old dances carry the names of the dead.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; composition with Fauré from 1897, counterpoint with André Gedalge
Les Apaches: Ricardo Viñes, Maurice Delage, Tristan Klingsor, Michel-Dimitri Calvocoressi and other musicians, writers and painters
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum preserving his piano and collections
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber music and piano works; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: Ravel, as remembered by his friend M. D. Calvocoressi

composer.background:
Ravel was born in Ciboure, across the harbour from Saint-Jean-de-Luz, to Marie Delouart, a Basque woman who had lived in Madrid, and Pierre-Joseph Ravel, a Swiss-born engineer. The family moved to Paris when Maurice was three months old. His father encouraged music as well as an interest in machinery; his mother’s songs gave him an early acquaintance with Spanish idioms. Basque ancestry and Spanish musical theatre remained distinct resources: the uneven pulse of the Piano Trio differs from the habanera of the Rapsodie espagnole. He returned to the Basque coast for holidays and composition, but received his musical education in Paris.

He entered the Conservatoire in 1889, initially as a pianist, and studied with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot. Failure to win the required prizes cost him his place in 1895. Readmitted in 1897 to Fauré’s composition class, he also learnt counterpoint from André Gedalge. Fauré encouraged the individual ear without relaxing the demands of construction; Gedalge supplied the discipline behind the fugues and independent inner parts. Ravel did not become a virtuoso pianist. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, introduced much of the difficult piano music, including Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit.
